episode_title: Tax News Now Ep. 24 - Before You Shake Hands: Hidden Tax Traps in Partnership Buyouts with Brian Lovett

real_qa.q: What hidden tax consequences arise from partnership liability relief in a buyout under Subchapter K?
real_qa.r: When a partner sells their interest and is relieved of partnership debt, that debt relief counts as part of the amount realized on the sale. If a partner has a negative capital account of $500,000 propped up by debt and receives $1 million from a buyout, they may actually owe tax on $1.5 million in gain—the $1 million received plus the $500,000 debt relief—rather than just the $1 million they thought they were receiving.
real_qa.requete: partnership liability relief tax consequences Section 751

real_qa.q: How does Section 751 hot asset recapture affect the tax treatment of a partnership interest sale?
real_qa.r: Under Section 751, unrealized receivables and inventory items in a partnership must be recaptured as ordinary income, not capital gain. A partner selling their interest may find that what they believed would be 20% capital gains tax becomes much higher because a portion of the sale price gets allocated to these hot assets, resulting in ordinary income treatment and potentially tax owed with no corresponding cash received in the current year.
real_qa.requete: Section 751 hot assets partnership interest sale ordinary income

real_qa.q: What is the difference between a cross-purchase and a partnership redemption in structuring a partner buyout?
real_qa.r: In a cross-purchase, remaining partners buy the exiting partner's interest directly outside the partnership; this is a closed transaction and the partner exits immediately. In a redemption, the partnership itself rebuys the interest under Section 736, and the exiting partner continues to receive K-1 forms and either guaranteed payments or distributive share until all payments are made, which can span multiple years and defer the 734B basis adjustment.
real_qa.requete: cross-purchase vs partnership redemption Section 736 buyout

real_qa.q: When should a Section 754 election be made in a partnership buyout to protect the acquiring partner from double taxation?
real_qa.r: A Section 754 election (specifically Section 743(b)) should be made when a partner buys into a partnership at fair market value to create a stepped-up asset basis, ensuring the gain is taxed once to the departing partner rather than twice—once on departure and again when the partnership later sells assets. Without the election, the new partner who bought in at fair value would still owe tax on that gain if the partnership sells assets shortly after.
real_qa.requete: Section 754 743b election partnership step-up basis double taxation

real_qa.q: Why do installment sales of partnership interests create unexpected tax bills when Section 751 hot assets are present?
real_qa.r: When a partnership interest is sold on an installment basis, unrealized receivables and inventory items under Section 751 must still be recaptured as ordinary income in the year of sale, regardless of when the cash is received. This creates a situation where the partner owes tax on recapture items with no corresponding cash payment, requiring funds to be available by the April 15 tax deadline.
real_qa.requete: installment sale partnership interest Section 751 recapture timing tax bill

guest.bio_context: Brian Lovett is a CPA and attorney with extensive experience working with business owners and real estate investors. He leads Witham's real estate strategic tax planning team and has deep expertise in partnership structures, buyouts, and tax deferral strategies.

real_quote: Partners don't often think about the impact of partnership liabilities. Debt allocated to a partner is part of their basis, and when they sell their interest, they're also relieved of that debt, which is part of the amount realized on the sale.
key_stats: Section 751 governs hot asset recapture as ordinary income in partnership interest sales
Section 754 election (743b adjustment) allows stepped-up basis to prevent double taxation on partnership asset sales
Section 736 bifurcates partnership redemptions into two payment types (A and B payments) with different tax treatment
Negative capital accounts propped up by partnership debt create hidden tax gain when relieved through buyout
Installment sales of partnership interests trigger full Section 751 recapture in year of sale, regardless of cash receipt timing
734b adjustment timing in redemptions is deferred until the exiting partner's capital account is over-distributed
